justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook with modest upward drift over longer horizons. For the 1-day estimate of 1037, I was anchoring closely to what appeared to be the prevailing level at the time of the forecast, assuming mean-reverting behavior over very short timeframes with minimal directional conviction. The 1-week estimate of 1040 reflects only a slight upward nudge, consistent with a modest positive drift assumption but not a strong directional view. The 1-month estimate of 1050 extends that gentle drift further, essentially assuming a low-volatility environment where the series trends marginally higher without major disruption.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated primarily to historical volatility at each respective horizon. Daily intervals are naturally tighter because there is less time for compounding uncertainty to accumulate. As the horizon extends to a week and then a month, the uncertainty bands widen substantially — from a roughly 55-point range at 1 day to a 100-point range at 1 month — reflecting the square-root-of-time scaling that typically governs financial or economic volatility. I also factored in that longer horizons introduce more regime uncertainty, meaning structural shifts in the underlying dynamics become increasingly plausible.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected shock — such as a sudden policy change, adverse macroeconomic data release, or liquidity event — could drive the series well below 1010 even within a single day. On the upside, a positive catalyst or short squeeze dynamic could propel values above 1065 quickly. At the monthly horizon, the tails are particularly fat relative to my stated interval, meaning that events like central bank policy pivots, geopolitical developments, or structural data revisions could easily push the outcome outside the 940–1160 range.

It is also worth noting that my confidence intervals represent 90% coverage, meaning I am explicitly acknowledging a 10% probability that outcomes fall outside those bounds. In practice, real-world distributions often have heavier tails than assumed, so the true probability of extreme outcomes may be somewhat higher than my stated intervals imply. Forecast users should treat the outer bounds as soft guardrails rather than hard limits.
